screens.title: The Fundamentals of CI/CD Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: In this introduction we will set a shared view of CI and CD and why they matter. Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery change how teams think about code changes: instead of long, risky integration events, small frequent merges trigger automated builds and tests. This automation reduces surprises, shortens feedback loops, and keeps the main branch in a deployable state. You will hear how Continuous Deployment differs by removing the manual release gate and why that requires very mature testing and monitoring. A concrete example: imagine a small bug fix pushed by one developer that is automatically built, tested, packaged as an artifact, and placed in a registry ready for release. With Continuous Delivery you can choose when to release that artifact; with Continuous Deployment it would be released immediately after the checks pass. A common misconception is that automation replaces human judgment; instead it augments it by removing repetitive steps and surfacing issues earlier. By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain the pipeline stages, justify the benefits, and spot common anti-patterns that undermine trust in automation.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson: CI, CD, pipeline stages, and common traps

The Fundamentals of CI/CD Pipelines

Understand how automation transforms commits into tested, deployable artifacts and how delivery choices affect risk and speed.

Why this matters

Faster feedback, fewer integration crises, and predictable releases let teams move confidently and respond to users quickly.

Practical outcome

You will be able to map a pipeline, choose CD vs CDP, and identify common failures to fix first.

Explore Key Topics
CI: Integrate Often
Merge frequently, run builds and unit tests automatically so integration issues surface quickly.
CD: Ready-to-Release
Package and deploy to staging automatically; keep production releases gated for business control.
Pipelines & Artifacts
Build artifacts that represent deployable units and store them reliably for traceability and rollback.
Concept Map
Commit
Developer pushes changes to central repository
Build & Test
Automated build, unit tests, and quality checks
Package & Release
Artifact stored, deployed to staging or production
Tip: Think of the pipeline as a quality funnel: each stage narrows risk and increases confidence before release.

First, you will explain core principles and benefits of Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery, which means you can describe why frequent integration and automated preparation for release improve speed and reliability. Third, you will identify the key components and workflow of a typical CI/CD pipeline, so you can draw or outline the stages from source control to deployable artifact and to production. Fourth, you will recognize common anti-patterns and adoption challenges such as broken pipelines, flaky tests, and security gaps, and propose pragmatic first fixes. Each objective pairs knowledge with a small practical milestone so you leave with both understanding and a checklist to apply to your projects.

screens.title: What is Continuous Integration?
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Integration is a development practice where team members frequently merge their code changes into a shared repository, and each merge triggers an automated build and test sequence. The central claim is simple: integrate early and often so integration problems are small and fast to fix. For example, if two developers change adjacent logic in a web handler, frequent integration catches their conflict within hours instead of weeks. A common misconception is that CI is only about running unit tests; in reality CI encompasses building, running unit tests, and executing quick static checks that ensure the main branch remains deployable. Practically, CI is enforced by automating the build and test steps on every commit and by protecting the main branch so only passing changes are merged. One useful mental model is to think of CI as the team's immediate feedback loop: it tells you whether a change compiles and passes the basic quality gates. A takeaway question: how would you structure CI to surface integration errors within 30 minutes of a commit? What is Continuous Integration? means integrate frequently; run automated builds and tests so the main branch stays deployable and conflicts are small.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and an everyday example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is Continuous Integration?
Core Concept

Continuous Integration explained

CI means merging often, building automatically, and running tests to keep the codebase healthy and deployable.

Key points
  • Automate build and unit tests on every commit to the central repo.
  • Integrate small changes frequently to isolate conflicts quickly.
  • Protect main branch so only passing changes are merged.
Key Takeaway

CI is the early-warning system for your codebase — it makes integration small and cheap to fix.

Example: small web handler
Scenario
Two developers update a request handler. With CI, each push triggers a build and unit tests that catch a breaking change within minutes.
Common misconception
Misbelief
CI is just running tests. Reality: CI is building, testing, and ensuring the main branch stays deployable.
Check your understanding
  • What minimum checks would you run on every commit to catch integration errors early?
  • How does protecting the main branch support team confidence?

screens.title: How Continuous Delivery works
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Delivery automates everything required to bring a build to a release-ready state while keeping the final production deployment as a manual decision. The claim to remember is that CD makes every change deployable at any time, but deployment timing remains under human control. Practically, after a CI build passes unit tests and quick checks, CD orchestration packages the application into an artifact, runs integration and acceptance tests, and deploys to staging or pre-production. Teams then review staging, perform exploratory tests or business validations, and approve the release window. For example, a team may automatically deploy every green build to a staging slot each night but require a manual sign-off before switching traffic in production. A common mistake is treating CD as merely scripted deployments; instead it is a set of verified steps and gates that maintain readiness. Takeaway: design CD so the artifact is immutable and traceable, and place manual approval where business risk or compliance demands human judgment. How Continuous Delivery works means cd keeps changes always ready for release by automating packaging and staging while preserving a manual production gate for business control.. In practical terms, from successful build to a release-ready artifact — with a manual gate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Continuous Delivery
Process

Daily flow for Continuous Delivery

1
Build & Unit Test
Automated checks ensure the artifact compiles and basic tests pass.
2
Package Artifact
Create immutable artifact and store in registry for traceability.
3
Deploy to Staging
Run integration and acceptance tests in a production-like environment.
Key Takeaway

CD makes each passing build ready for release and provides control over when to deploy to production.

Concrete example
Nightly staging deploy
Every green main build deploys to staging at 02:00. QA performs exploratory testing and a release manager approves production promotion during business hours.
Misconception
Misbelief
CD is not 'set and forget' automation. It requires disciplined testing, immutable artifacts, and deliberate gates where necessary.

screens.title: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment share the goal of fast, reliable releases, but they differ on whether production deployment is automated. Continuous Delivery ensures every change is built, tested, and packaged so it is ready to release. The final step into production remains manual. This preserves business control and allows approvals, release windows, or compliance checks. Continuous Deployment automates that last step: every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically. The benefit is speed and immediate value delivery; the cost is that it requires very strong automated tests, robust monitoring, and fast rollback mechanisms. A useful example: a customer-facing bug fix can reach users within minutes under Continuous Deployment, while Continuous Delivery might wait for a scheduled release after a human review. A common misconception is that Continuous Deployment removes responsibility; in truth it shifts responsibility toward improving automated quality gates and observability. Consider which model aligns with your risk tolerance, testing maturity, and business needs before choosing a path. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment means cd = ready-to-release with manual production gate. cdp = automatic production deployment after passing pipeline checks.. In practical terms, trade-offs: human control vs full automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: CD = ready-to-release with manual production gate. CDP = automatic production deployment after passing pipeline checks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Delivery vs Deployment
Continuous Delivery

Ready for production with a manual gate

CD automates packaging and staging but keeps human approval before production. This balances speed with business control.

When to choose CD
  • When releases require legal approval or a business window.
  • When your tests are strong but you want a last human check.
Continuous Deployment

Fully automated production deployment

CDP deploys every passing change automatically. It requires rigorous tests, monitoring, and rollback strategies to be safe.

When to choose CDP
  • When you can trust automated tests and observability to catch regressions quickly.
  • When delivering small changes rapidly is core to your product strategy.
Concrete contrast

Example: a bug fix under CD waits for release manager approval; under CDP it reaches users automatically after passing tests. The choice depends on risk tolerance and testing maturity.

screens.title: Typical CI/CD Pipeline Stages
screens.narratorSegment: A typical CI/CD pipeline is a sequence of stages that transform source code into a deployable artifact and then into running software. Think of it as a checklist that must be green before proceeding. Common stages include: source control where commits trigger pipelines; build which compiles or packages code; unit test for fast feedback; integration and acceptance tests for behavioral checks; artifact creation where a Docker image or package is stored; deployment to staging for production-like validation; and finally promotion to production with or without a manual gate. For a Flask app, the build might create a Docker image, unit tests check handlers, and integration tests exercise endpoints against a test database. A frequent misconception is that more stages always equal better quality. In practice, each stage adds time and complexity, so choose tests that provide high signal-to-noise. Design pipelines so failing fast is possible; prioritize quick unit tests early and longer system tests later. Takeaway: map stages, measure stage duration, and optimize where time-to-feedback is longest. Typical CI/CD Pipeline Stages means source → build → unit test → integration tests → package artifact → staging → production promotion; optimize for fast feedback early.. In practical terms, a practical stage-by-stage checklist you can apply to any app. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Source → Build → Unit Test → Integration Tests → Package Artifact → Staging → Production promotion; optimize for fast feedback early.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Pipeline Stages

Pipeline stages (numbered)

  1. Source Control: commits trigger pipelines and provide traceability.
  2. Build: compile or assemble artifacts like Docker images.
  3. Unit Tests: fast checks for logic correctness.
  4. Integration / Acceptance Tests: verify component interactions.
  5. Package / Artifact Creation: produce immutable deployables.
  6. Deploy to Staging: run production-like validations.
  7. Production Promotion: manual or automatic deployment to live users.
Tip: Track stage duration and flakiness; long-running or flaky stages are the usual bottlenecks.
Concrete example: Flask app
Build step
Create Docker image, install dependencies, run lint.
Test steps
Unit tests for business logic, integration tests against test DB, health checks.
Key Takeaway

Organize stages to fail fast and keep deployable artifacts immutable for traceability and rollback.

screens.title: Automated Testing in CI/CD
screens.narratorSegment: Automated testing is the practice of using software to run checks and compare actual outcomes with expected outcomes; it is essential to CI/CD reliability. In pipeline terms, different tests play different roles: unit tests are fast and focused on individual functions; integration tests check component interactions; acceptance tests validate user-facing behavior; and smoke tests ensure basic functionality after deployment. The practical effect is that each test type provides a filter: unit tests catch small regressions quickly, integration tests catch interface mismatches, and acceptance tests confirm business requirements. A concrete example: a unit test checks that a price calculation returns correct totals, while an integration test ensures the pricing service and database communicate correctly. A common misconception is that 100% test coverage equals safety. Coverage is a metric, not a guarantee; tests must assert meaningful behaviors. The takeaway is to design layered tests with quick guards early and deeper checks later in the pipeline, to protect speed and reliability simultaneously. Automated Testing in CI/CD means layer tests so fast checks run first and longer system tests run later, preserving fast feedback while ensuring correctness.. In practical terms, why testing is the backbone of trusted automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Automated Testing

Test types and purpose

  • Unit tests: fast, validate single functions or classes.
  • Integration tests: verify multiple components working together.
  • Acceptance tests: simulate user journeys and business rules.
  • Smoke tests: quick health checks after deployment.
Tip: Run unit tests on every commit and schedule longer integration suites on push to main to balance speed and coverage.
Concrete example
Price calculation
Unit test asserts expected totals. Integration test calls pricing API with test DB to verify real interactions.
Misconception
Misbelief
High coverage alone is not safety; tests must be meaningful, deterministic, and maintained to be effective.

screens.title: Artifacts and Packaging
screens.narratorSegment: An artifact is a deployable component produced by the build process, such as a Docker image, compiled executable, or packaged library. The essential property is immutability: once created, an artifact represents a specific, testable snapshot of the application. This immutability enables traceability — you can match a production deployment back to the exact artifact and the commit that produced it — and it simplifies rollback because you redeploy a previously built artifact. For example, a Docker image tagged with a build number is an immutable artifact that can be deployed to staging or production. A common misunderstanding is treating deployment scripts as the artifact. In reality the artifact is the package the scripts deploy, not the scripts themselves. Best practice is to store artifacts in a registry with metadata that records the originating commit, test results, and build environment. Key takeaway: treat artifacts as first-class, immutable outputs that carry the provenance needed for safe releases and rollbacks. Artifacts and Packaging means produce immutable, traceable artifacts and store them in a registry with metadata for reliable promotion and rollback.. In practical terms, what an artifact is and why immutability matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Artifacts & Packaging

What is an artifact?

A deployable, immutable output of the build process, stored with metadata for traceability.

Examples: Docker images, compiled binaries, packaged libraries.
Why immutability matters: it ensures exact reproducibility and simple rollbacks.
Registry practices: store artifacts with build numbers, commit IDs, and test status.
Key Takeaway

Treat artifacts as canonical deployable units with clear provenance to enable reliable promotions and rollbacks.

Concrete scenario
Docker image tagging
Tag images with build ID and commit hash. Store in a registry so staging and production use the exact same image.
Misconception
Misbelief
Treating deployment scripts as artifacts leads to non-reproducible releases; separate the artifact from deployment logic.

screens.title: Common Anti-patterns and Challenges
screens.narratorSegment: Pipelines fail for predictable reasons and restoring trust starts by fixing the frequent culprits. A broken pipeline is the most damaging anti-pattern: when builds or tests regularly fail, teams start bypassing automation and the benefits vanish. Root causes include flaky tests, unstable test environments, brittle configuration, and neglected maintenance. Another anti-pattern is over-automation without sufficient tests; automating a flawed process simply speeds up failures. Security gaps are also common; if secrets and vulnerability scanning are absent, automation can propagate risks faster. For example, flaky integration tests that depend on shared mutable state will cause intermittent failures and slow developer feedback. Priority fixes are stabilizing tests by isolating dependencies, making test data deterministic, and ensuring environments are reproducible. A practical approach is to mark flaky tests and quarantine them while you repair their determinism. Takeaway: measure pipeline health, fix the top flakiness sources first, and only then expand automation. narration.text: Pipelines fail for predictable reasons and restoring trust starts by fixing the frequent culprits. A broken pipeline is the most damaging anti-pattern: when builds or tests regularly fail, teams start bypassing automation and the benefits vanish. Broken Pipeline

screens.title: Monitoring, Rollbacks and Maturity
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring and rollback capability are essential to trusting automated deployments. When Continuous Deployment is in place, a bad change can reach users quickly; observability detects regressions and rollback tools restore service fast. Key signals include error rates, latency, and business metrics like checkout success. A concrete example: if a new release increases error rate by 5 percent, an automated rollback or traffic shift reduces user impact while the team investigates. Rollback strategies include redeploying a previous artifact, feature toggles to disable problematic functionality, and progressive traffic shifting to detect issues early. A common misconception is that monitoring only alerts you after users complain. In mature pipelines, automated alerts and automated rollbacks minimize user exposure. To progress in maturity, start with good logging and alerts, add automated canary deployments, and ensure artifacts and metadata support fast rollbacks. Starter template: pipeline_stages.md

Fill each stage with actions, outputs, and whether it is automated or manual under CD and CDP.

# Basic CI/CD Pipeline Stages for a Flask Application

## Stage 1: Source Code Management
Description: Commit triggers pipeline; record commit ID and branch.

## Stage 2: Build
Description: Create Docker image, install dependencies, run lint.

## Stage 3: Test
Description: Run unit tests (fast) and integration tests (slower).

## Stage 4: Package/Artifact Creation
Description: Tag and push image to registry with build metadata.

## Stage 5: Deploy to Staging (for CD/CDP)
Description: Deploy artifact to staging, run acceptance tests and smoke checks.

## Stage 6: Manual Approval (for CD)
Description: Release manager verifies and approves promotion to production.

## Stage 7: Deploy to Production (for CDP)
Description: Under CDP, promote artifact automatically after passing gates.
Guidance
  • For each stage, note the success signal (exit code, test pass, health check).
  • Decide whether the stage produces an artifact or simply a status report.
  • Mark slow or flaky stages to optimize later.
Key Takeaway

Design each stage with a clear exit condition and an explicit artifact or signal to hand to the next stage.

screens.title: Progressive Automation and Team Culture
screens.narratorSegment: Adopting CI/CD is as much cultural as it is technical. Progressive automation means starting with the smallest reliable automation and expanding step by step, ensuring each stage is stable before adding the next. Begin by running unit tests on every commit and protecting the main branch. Next automate packaging and artifact storage. Then add staging deployment and system tests. At each step, involve the team: developers, QA, release managers, and security. A concrete practice is to create a definition of 'pipeline health' that tracks build success rate, mean time to repair, and test flakiness. Misconception to avoid: automation will automatically speed development. Instead, automation speeds development only if the pipeline is trusted. Trust is built by reducing false positives, fixing flakiness, and making failures actionable. A final reflective question: what one stage would you stabilize first to regain team confidence in automation — unit tests, build reliability, or environment reproducibility? Progressive Automation and Team Culture means automate progressively, measure pipeline health, and grow trust by fixing flaky stages before adding more automation.. fullNarratorScript:
In this introduction we will set a shared view of CI and CD and why they matter. Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery change how teams think about code changes: instead of long, risky integration events, small frequent merges trigger automated builds and tests. This automation reduces surprises, shortens feedback loops, and keeps the main branch in a deployable state. You will hear how Continuous Deployment differs by removing the manual release gate and why that requires very mature testing and monitoring. A concrete example: imagine a small bug fix pushed by one developer that is automatically built, tested, packaged as an artifact, and placed in a registry ready for release. With Continuous Delivery you can choose when to release that artifact; with Continuous Deployment it would be released immediately after the checks pass. A common misconception is that automation replaces human judgment; instead it augments it by removing repetitive steps and surfacing issues earlier. By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain the pipeline stages, justify the benefits, and spot common anti-patterns that undermine trust in automation.

These objectives focus your learning on both concepts and practical skills. First, you will explain core principles and benefits of Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery, which means you can describe why frequent integration and automated preparation for release improve speed and reliability. Second, you will differentiate between Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment by identifying which stages are automated and which still require human approval, with examples that show the trade-offs. Third, you will identify the key components and workflow of a typical CI/CD pipeline, so you can draw or outline the stages from source control to deployable artifact and to production. Fourth, you will recognize common anti-patterns and adoption challenges such as broken pipelines, flaky tests, and security gaps, and propose pragmatic first fixes. Each objective pairs knowledge with a small practical milestone so you leave with both understanding and a checklist to apply to your projects.

Beyond conceptual understanding, practical habits make CI/CD work. You will practice mapping a pipeline for a small Flask application, listing each stage and what it accomplishes. This includes creating a source control step, a build step that produces an artifact, a test stage with unit and integration tests, packaging into a deployable form, and a staging deployment. You will also practice deciding where a manual approval fits in Continuous Delivery and what changes when moving to Continuous Deployment. A concrete exercise: create a pipeline_stages. md that explains each stage and whether the pipeline automates deployment to production. Finally, you will evaluate common failure modes and propose fixes such as stabilizing flaky tests, locking down secrets, and adding monitoring. These practices will let you progress from understanding to applying pipeline design in your next project.

Continuous Integration is a development practice where team members frequently merge their code changes into a shared repository, and each merge triggers an automated build and test sequence. The central claim is simple: integrate early and often so integration problems are small and fast to fix. For example, if two developers change adjacent logic in a web handler, frequent integration catches their conflict within hours instead of weeks. A common misconception is that CI is only about running unit tests; in reality CI encompasses building, running unit tests, and executing quick static checks that ensure the main branch remains deployable. Practically, CI is enforced by automating the build and test steps on every commit and by protecting the main branch so only passing changes are merged. One useful mental model is to think of CI as the team's immediate feedback loop: it tells you whether a change compiles and passes the basic quality gates. A takeaway question: how would you structure CI to surface integration errors within 30 minutes of a commit? What is Continuous Integration? means integrate frequently; run automated builds and tests so the main branch stays deployable and conflicts are small.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Continuous Delivery automates everything required to bring a build to a release-ready state while keeping the final production deployment as a manual decision. The claim to remember is that CD makes every change deployable at any time, but deployment timing remains under human control. Practically, after a CI build passes unit tests and quick checks, CD orchestration packages the application into an artifact, runs integration and acceptance tests, and deploys to staging or pre-production. Teams then review staging, perform exploratory tests or business validations, and approve the release window. For example, a team may automatically deploy every green build to a staging slot each night but require a manual sign-off before switching traffic in production. A common mistake is treating CD as merely scripted deployments; instead it is a set of verified steps and gates that maintain readiness. Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment share the goal of fast, reliable releases, but they differ on whether production deployment is automated. Continuous Delivery ensures every change is built, tested, and packaged so it is ready to release. The final step into production remains manual. This preserves business control and allows approvals, release windows, or compliance checks. Continuous Deployment automates that last step: every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically. The benefit is speed and immediate value delivery; the cost is that it requires very strong automated tests, robust monitoring, and fast rollback mechanisms. A useful example: a customer-facing bug fix can reach users within minutes under Continuous Deployment, while Continuous Delivery might wait for a scheduled release after a human review. Adopting CI/CD is as much cultural as it is technical. Progressive automation means starting with the smallest reliable automation and expanding step by step, ensuring each stage is stable before adding the next. Let's consolidate the main ideas. Continuous Integration means frequent merges and automated builds and tests so the main branch stays deployable. Continuous Delivery extends CI by preparing every change for release while keeping the final production deployment manual, which gives business control. Continuous Deployment goes further by automating production deployment for every passing change, but it requires robust tests and monitoring. A CI/CD pipeline is a sequence of stages from source to artifact to staging and production; artifacts should be immutable and stored with provenance. Automated tests are the backbone of reliable automation and should be layered to provide fast feedback early and deeper checks later. Finally, pipelines fail most often because of flaky tests, unstable environments, or insufficient observability. The takeaway is to automate progressively, stabilize failing stages first, and ensure monitoring and rollback strategies are in place.

Third, measure pipeline health and treat flaky tests as urgent technical debt; an unreliable pipeline defeats automation.
